headline: Mercedes-Benz VLE is an 8K living room on wheels with 350-mile range
summary: The 2028 Mercedes-Benz VLE redefines luxury travel with a 31.3-inch ultrawide 8K display, Dolby Atmos sound, and reclining massage seats, offering a premium experience for passengers.
details: Mercedes-Benz is set to launch the VLE, an electric "Grand Limousine" concept for 2028, aiming to make minivans cool. It promises a luxurious "living room on wheels" experience, featuring a 31.3-inch ultrawide 8K display and a 22-speaker Dolby Atmos sound system for second-row passengers.

Despite its minivan-like silhouette, the VLE is a substantial vehicle, measuring 216 inches long—10 inches longer than a GLS SUV. Its 49-inch internal ceiling height allows for easy movement inside the cabin, enhancing the spacious feel.

The VLE can be configured for up to eight passengers across three rows, but its most luxurious setup features two captain's chairs in the second row. These seats are heated, ventilated, and offer significant recline, prioritizing passenger comfort.

Two powertrains will be available: the VLE 300 (272 hp, FWD) and the VLE 400 4MATIC (416 hp, AWD). Both use a 115 kWh battery, providing an estimated 350 miles of EPA range. The 800-volt system allows for rapid charging, adding about 200 miles in just 15 minutes.

The second row is the heart of the VLE's luxury, offering a glass ceiling and the massive 8K display for entertainment. Passengers can stream content from Disney+ and YouTube, or connect external devices via an HDMI port.

For families, the 8K screen can split into two 15-inch 4K displays, allowing two passengers to watch different content simultaneously with individual Bluetooth headsets. Basic games are also available on the system.
The front cabin features Mercedes' MBUX Superscreen, comprising a 10.25-inch gauge cluster, a 14-inch central infotainment screen, and a 14-inch passenger display that can also stream media.

The Burmester 3D sound system with Dolby Atmos delivers an immersive audio experience. It dynamically reconfigures sound output based on the number and position of occupants, ensuring optimal acoustics for everyone.

headline: Claude Code ran --dangerously-skip-permissions on my production DB, nearly causing disaster
summary: A developer accidentally ran an AI coding assistant with dangerous permissions on a live database due to an environment misconfiguration, narrowly avoiding a major data loss. This incident highlights critical safety lessons for AI tool integration.
details: Last Tuesday, a multi-agent loop running Claude Code hit 12K KV writes/minute and froze due to a one-line counter bug. Tracing this issue revealed a much more critical problem at hand.

The developer had accidentally enabled --dangerously-skip-permissions on a Claude Code session, which was mistakenly pointing to a production database instead of staging. This was due to a misconfigured environment file reference.

The ADD COLUMN migration thankfully prevented data loss, but the flag's true meaning was misunderstood: it removes the critical human confirmation step before execution. This is far more severe than just skipping popups.

To prevent future incidents, the developer implemented a deny rule in .claude/settings.json, specifically blocking production database commands. This rule is more specific than any allow rules, ensuring local calls still function.

Over two weeks post-fix, Claude attempted zero production DB commands, with three deny events logged from ambiguous prompts. This confirmed the effectiveness of the settings.json allowlist in preventing unintended actions.

Additional layers of protection were added, including a separate git worktree for migration work containing only staging credentials, and a CLAUDE.md file instructing Claude to ask before touching production.

A key caveat with CLAUDE.md is that its instructions can lose weight in long sessions as context grows. Therefore, any critical instructions must be explicitly restated within the prompt itself for maximum safety.
